edge.title: The flat that doesn't exist
edge.setup: You find a 2BHK listed well under market rate. The 'owner' is warm, shares photos, an Aadhaar copy, even a video walkthrough. He's posted abroad / in the army / transferred to Delhi, so a 'caretaker' will hand over keys. He just needs the token advance today because three others are interested. Everything checks out except one thing: you have not stood inside that flat.
edge.tell: Money is moving before a key has turned in a lock you touched.
move: Never transfer anything before physically standing inside the flat with someone who can open it.
Match the name on the EC/khata or tax receipt to the person's ID yourself — don't accept a forwarded photo.
If pressure to pay today appears, treat that as the scam announcing itself, not as competition.
edge.why: Documents are cheap to forge and free to send. Physical access is not. Every version of this scam works by substituting a convincing artefact (ID scan, video, rent agreement PDF) for the one costly thing a real owner always has: the ability to let you in.
edge.variants: Same shape: used-car 'in transit from Pune', PG deposits, farmland plots 'near the new airport', pet sales with a transport fee.

lens.name: Goodhart's Law
lens.one_line: When a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring what it used to.
lens.detail: Any number used to judge people will be optimised directly, often by routes that bypass the thing the number was standing in for. Not usually by cheating — by honest, rational effort aimed at the metric rather than the goal, because the metric is what's rewarded.
elsewhere: Police judged on cases closed may book easier cases and discourage hard complaints.
Schools judged on pass rates quietly move weak students out before the exam.
Support teams judged on ticket-closing time close tickets fast, unresolved.
lens.test: What number are these people judged on, and what's the cheapest way to move it that doesn't involve doing the actual job?
lens.today: Residents across south Bengaluru are asking for the ₹900 crore OMR–Indiranagar–Madiwala flyover tender to be cancelled and for public transport to be funded instead. Their argument is a Goodhart one: if the target is vehicle speed on one stretch, a flyover scores well, but the number that matters to you is door-to-door time for the most people. When a project is justified by a proxy, ask what the proxy was standing in for.

moved.what: Overnight rain waterlogged roads and disrupted the morning traffic in Bengaluru (DD News).
moved.so_what: Rain-hit mornings are when the bus-plus-Metro fallback matters most. If more rain is forecast tomorrow, leave earlier or check your route before you start.

moved.what: The Commissioner of Metro Rail Safety has begun inspecting the Pink Line, and BMTC has proposed five feeder routes at a 10-minute frequency (Swarajya, The Hindu, Times of India).
moved.so_what: The inspection precedes opening, but no opening date was reported. Do not change your commute yet; watch for the final feeder route list, which decides whether the last mile works for you.

moved.what: BMTC plans to share real-time bus data with mobility platforms and is exploring tap-to-pay and flat fares (The Hindu, Moneycontrol).
moved.so_what: If it goes through, live bus arrivals could show up in the apps you already use. It is a plan for now, so nothing to change yet.

moved.what: Residents held human chains against the ₹900 crore OMR–Indiranagar–Madiwala flyover tender and asked for Metro and bus upgrades instead (The News Minute, Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: If you commute on that corridor, expect construction disruption if the tender proceeds. A public comment or ward meeting is the lever; it is where the decision can still move.

moved.what: Times of India reports that a 'super El Niño' threatens India's coffee harvest, with Karnataka facing a 15 to 20% output slump.
moved.so_what: Expect upward pressure on coffee prices over the coming months, filter coffee powder included. Not a reason to stock up, just not to be surprised by the next price revision.

carry_over.prompt: A buyer says his app is acting up and asks you to scan a QR code or approve a request so the money lands in your account. What is the one thing in that flow that tells you money is leaving, not arriving?
carry_over.answer: You were asked for your UPI PIN to receive money.
